0.title: The Gospel and the Slave: Paul's Letter to Philemon
0.overview:
Philemon is the most personal of Paul's surviving letters — a private request from a prisoner to a friend on behalf of a runaway slave. Twenty-five verses. No doctrinal argument, no community disputes, no eschatological vision. Just a man writing to a man about a third man, in the most careful and emotionally loaded prose Paul ever produced. That it was preserved in the canon at all — and that Marcion included it in his truncated collection — tells us that the early church recognized something here that went beyond private correspondence.

The situation is this: Onesimus, a slave belonging to the wealthy Colossian Christian Philemon, had run away. By Roman law, a runaway slave was a thief — he had stolen himself, depriving his master of the economic value of his labor, and possibly taken money or property in the process (v. 18 implies some kind of financial debt). He had somehow — the details are not given — come into contact with Paul, then imprisoned in Rome (or possibly Ephesus), and had been converted. He had become genuinely useful to Paul in his imprisonment. And Paul was sending him back, letter in hand.

The letter is a masterpiece of rhetorical strategy. Paul never commands Philemon to free Onesimus — he appeals, he hints, he presses, he places moral weight. He frames Onesimus as his own child (v. 10), his very heart (v. 12), a beloved brother (v. 16). He writes a personal financial guarantee for any debt (vv. 18–19). He expresses confidence that Philemon will do 'even more than I say' (v. 21). And he announces that he is coming to stay (v. 22). By the end of the letter, Philemon cannot refuse without refusing Paul himself — and refusing Paul means refusing the gospel they both serve.

The deepest theological claim of the letter is in v. 16: Onesimus is to be received 'no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother — both in the flesh and in the Lord.' The gospel does not erase social realities; it transforms them. Onesimus is still a man with a history, a legal status, a relationship with Philemon that has been damaged. But he is now a brother — in the flesh (as a human being) and in the Lord (as a fellow Christian). These two dimensions must operate simultaneously. Paul is not calling for the abolition of slavery in this letter; he is doing something more radical in the long run — he is planting a theological seed that makes slavery incompatible with Christian brotherhood.

1.title: Grace and a Brother: The Complete Letter
1.overview:
The letter unfolds in five movements: greeting (vv. 1–3), thanksgiving that both commends Philemon and establishes the relational capital Paul will spend (vv. 4–7), the appeal for Onesimus (vv. 8–16), the direct request and its financial guarantee (vv. 17–22), and final greetings (vv. 23–25). The movement from thanksgiving to appeal is calculated: Paul is building Philemon up before he asks anything of him, and the qualities he praises — love, faith, refreshing the hearts of the saints — are precisely the qualities the request will require.

The word splanchna (heart, deep affections — literally the inward parts, the seat of emotion in ancient physiology) appears three times and functions as the letter's emotional spine: in v. 7, the saints' hearts have been refreshed by Philemon; in v. 12, Paul sends Onesimus who is Paul's own heart; in v. 20, Paul asks Philemon to refresh Paul's heart. The chain is a deliberate literary strategy: establish Philemon as a heart-refresher, identify Onesimus as Paul's heart, ask Philemon to refresh Paul's heart by receiving Onesimus. The emotional argument is built into the structure.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul opens not as 'apostle' (his standard self-identification) but as 'a prisoner of Christ Jesus.' This is a rhetorical choice: he has apostolic authority over Philemon, but he is deliberately not invoking it. The authority he is withholding becomes the implied pressure behind every appeal that follows — Paul could command, but chooses not to. The introduction of Timothy as co-sender further softens the authoritative posture; this is not an apostolic directive but a personal request from a prisoner and his associate.
verseByVerse.theology: The address to 'the church in your house' ensures that Philemon's response will be witnessed. This is not a private matter between two men; it is a matter of the community's gospel integrity. The whole church will know what Philemon does with Onesimus. Paul's decision to address the letter publicly is itself a form of social pressure — Philemon cannot read this letter in private and quietly refuse. The gospel Paul preaches creates communities of accountability, not just individual transformations.
verseByVerse.examples: The 'prisoner of Christ Jesus' self-identification is one of Paul's most deliberate rhetorical moves. He is in chains; he is asking a favor; he identifies himself by his weakness rather than his authority. Every minister who makes a pastoral appeal from vulnerability rather than position is following this pattern. Then: Paul in Roman chains writing to a prosperous householder in Colossae. Now: a pastor who needs a wealthy member to make a costly decision, choosing persuasion over positional leverage — and achieving more by the former than the latter.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a prisoner for Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker and Apphia our sister and Archippus our fellow soldier, and the church in your house: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A prisoner of Christ Jesus' — not 'apostle,' not 'slave of God and apostle' as in Titus, not 'slave of Christ Jesus' as in Philippians. Paul is in a Roman prison on account of Christ; he opens with his weakness, not his authority. The rhetorical strategy of the whole letter is compressed into this phrase: I appeal to you as a man in chains, not as your superior. 'Philemon our beloved fellow worker' (agapētō kai synergō) — both adjectives are significant: agapētos (beloved) establishes the affectional bond; synergos (fellow worker, co-laborer) establishes equality rather than hierarchy — Paul and Philemon work together in the gospel. This parity will matter when Paul makes his appeal. 'Apphia our sister' — almost certainly Philemon's wife; her inclusion means she too must consent to what is asked. 'Archippus our fellow soldier' (systratiōtēs) — the military metaphor of shared combat; Archippus is mentioned in Colossians 4:17 as having a ministry to fulfil. 'The church in your house' — the congregation that meets in Philemon's home; the letter is addressed to them collectively, making Philemon's response a matter of communal witness, not private decision.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The thanksgiving is genuine — Paul does not manufacture flattery — but it is also calculated. He commends in Philemon exactly the qualities that the request ahead will require: love, faith toward all the saints, and the habit of refreshing the hearts (splanchna) of God's people. Having established these qualities as real characteristics of Philemon, Paul can later appeal to them: this is who you are; now be it toward Onesimus. The thanksgiving sets up the request without saying so.
verseByVerse.theology: 'The sharing of your faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ' (v. 6) — the word koinōnia (sharing, fellowship, partnership) will return in v. 17 as koinōnon (partner): 'if you consider me your partner.' The koinōnia of faith creates the koinōnia of obligation. Because Philemon shares the faith with Paul, he shares the obligations that faith produces. The theological logic of the whole letter is latent in this thanksgiving: gospel partnership means shared responsibility for those the gospel has reached.
verseByVerse.examples: The pastoral wisdom of vv. 4–7 is this: before you ask anything difficult of someone, honestly name what is true and good about them. Paul is not flattering Philemon; he is reminding Philemon of who Philemon already is, so that the request ahead is not an imposition from outside but a call to be consistent with what is already inside. Good pastoral persuasion always works this way: not 'you should become something you aren't' but 'you are already this — now live it here.'

verseByVerse.quote: I thank my God always when I remember you in my prayers, because I hear of your love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints, and I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ. For I have derived much joy and comfort from your love, my brother, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you' — ta splanchna tōn hagiōn anapepautai. The word splanchna (inward parts, bowels) was the ancient physiological seat of deep emotion — roughly equivalent to the modern 'heart' in affective meaning. Paul uses this word three times in the letter: here in v. 7 (Philemon has refreshed the saints' splanchna), in v. 12 (Onesimus is Paul's own splanchna), and in v. 20 (Paul asks Philemon to refresh Paul's splanchna). The three uses are a deliberate literary chain: Philemon is established as a refresher of hearts; Paul's heart is identified with Onesimus; therefore, Philemon refreshing Paul's heart means receiving Onesimus. The emotional argument is architecturally built into the letter's structure, not merely expressed in sentiment. 'The sharing of your faith' (hē koinōnia tēs pisteōs sou) — the noun koinōnia (fellowship, sharing, partnership) will reappear in v. 17 as koinōnon (partner): the shared faith creates the shared obligations of what Paul is about to ask.

Verse 6 is the most exegetically difficult in the letter: "I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ." Three elements need unpacking. Koinōnia tēs pisteōs (the sharing/fellowship of your faith) — this can mean either the faith you share with others (faith as communicated) or the fellowship that your faith produces (the relational network the gospel creates). In context, where Paul is about to appeal to the relational obligations that shared faith generates, the second sense fits better: the community of faith Philemon inhabits. Energēs (effective, active, at work — from energeia, energy/working power) — Paul prays that this fellowship will actually do something, will become operative in practice rather than merely potential. Epignōsis pantos agathou tou en hēmin (full knowledge of every good thing that is in us) — epignōsis is the deep, transformative knowing (as in 2 Pet 1:2–3, "grace and peace be multiplied to you in the epignōsis of God") rather than mere intellectual awareness; "every good thing in us" refers to the gifts, graces, and calling that Christ has placed in the community by the Spirit (most commentators read "in us" as the Christian community, not just Paul). The overall sense: Paul prays that the practical expression of Philemon's gospel-fellowship will lead him to a deeper recognition of all that Christ has already deposited in him — and that this recognition will produce action. It is a prayer that Philemon's theology will catch up with his practice, and his practice with his theology. For the preacher: the verse is a prayer for gospel-consistency, the alignment of what Philemon believes with what Philemon does when the gospel costs something.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This is the heart of the letter. Paul moves from the warmth of the thanksgiving into the appeal itself, carefully managing every word. He establishes what he is NOT doing (commanding by apostolic authority) before establishing what he IS doing (appealing out of love). He introduces Onesimus with the most intimate possible language — his child, his heart, his very self. He handles the delicate history (the offense, the separation) with hints rather than accusations. And he plants the theological seed that will determine how everything must be resolved: Onesimus is now a beloved brother, in the flesh and in the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 16 is the theological center of the letter and one of the most radical statements in the New Testament regarding the social implications of the gospel: Onesimus is to be received 'no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother — both in the flesh and in the Lord' (en sarki kai en kyriō). The two-level phrase is deliberate: en sarki means in the sphere of the physical, social, economic reality; en kyriō means in the sphere of union with Christ. The gospel does not collapse the distinction between these two spheres (Onesimus still has a history with Philemon; the legal reality of Roman slavery still exists) but it transforms what both mean. To be a brother en sarki is to acknowledge Onesimus's full humanity in the everyday, practical realm. To be a brother en kyriō is to acknowledge that in Christ there is neither slave nor free (Gal 3:28). Both are now true simultaneously.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul's refusal to command (v. 8) while applying overwhelming moral pressure (vv. 9–16) is one of the most sophisticated pieces of pastoral correspondence in history. He wants Philemon's action to be freely chosen — 'that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord' (v. 14). Forced compliance with the gospel's demands is not the same as gospel-transformed response. A congregation that does the right thing because the pastor commanded it is less transformed than one that does it because they have understood the gospel's logic. Paul is willing to invest a whole letter's worth of argument to ensure that Philemon's choice is genuinely his own. Then: a runaway slave brought back by the power of a letter. Now: a reconciliation between estranged Christians — the person who has wronged another, the person who has been wronged, and the third party who believes that their shared faith requires a different outcome than the natural one.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required, yet for love's sake I prefer to appeal to you — I, Paul, an old man and now a prisoner also for Christ Jesus — I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I became in my imprisonment. (Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me.) I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart. I would have been glad to keep him with me, in order that he might serve me on your behalf during my imprisonment for the gospel, but I preferred to do nothing without your consent, in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord. For this perhaps is why he was separated from you for a while, that you might have him back forever, no longer as a slave but better than a slave, as a dear brother — especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'I, Paul, an old man' (presbytēs) — this word occasionally causes confusion because a similar word, presbeutēs (ambassador), differs only slightly in spelling. Some interpreters (Lightfoot, NEB margin) suggest Paul means 'ambassador,' invoking an official title. The manuscript tradition is clear: presbytēs = old man, not ambassador. Paul is appealing from personal frailty and age, not official authority — which is precisely the rhetorical strategy of this section. 'Onesimus' — the name means 'useful' or 'profitable' in Greek (onēsimos). Paul's wordplay in v. 11 is a deliberate theological pun: 'formerly he was achrestos (useless) to you, but now he is indeed euchrestos (truly useful) to you and to me.' The word achrestos also sounds like aChristos (without Christ), and euchrestos like euChristos (with/in Christ, or Christ-like). A slave named Useful who was useless, converted by the gospel, now fulfils his own name: the wordplay on 'Onesimus' is the letter's theological argument in miniature. 'Sending my very heart' (ta ema splanchna) — the second of three uses; Paul identifies himself so completely with Onesimus that to send Onesimus back is to send Paul. 'He was separated from you for a while' (apechōristhē) — the passive voice hints at divine providence without asserting it boldly; Paul is not claiming God caused Onesimus to run away, but that God can be seen working in the separation. 'Forever' (aiōnion) — the eschatological weight of the word is deliberate: the renewed relationship transcends the temporary disruption; it is permanent and ultimate. 'In the flesh and in the Lord' (en sarki kai en kyriō) — in the practical, social, economic reality of daily life, and in union with Christ: both simultaneously. The gospel doesn't erase the human dimension but transforms it.

A background question preachers will face: Was Onesimus actually a runaway slave? The traditional reading — dominant from Chrysostom through the Reformation and still the majority today — holds that Onesimus fled after wronging Philemon, found his way to Paul in Rome or Ephesus, was converted, and is now being sent back. This reading fits v. 18 ("if he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything"), the language of "separated" (v. 15), and the entire logic of Paul's appeal. A minority reading, associated with Peter Lampe (1985) and others, proposes that Onesimus was not a fugitive but a slave who had wronged his master and sought out Paul as an amicus domini — a respected friend of the owner who could mediate the dispute before Onesimus returned. This was a recognized social practice in Roman law: a slave could take refuge with an influential friend of the household to seek intercession rather than face direct punishment. On this reading, Onesimus was not a thief but a petitioner, and Paul is fulfilling the mediating role, albeit as a converted apostle whose letter goes far beyond standard arbitration. The preacher does not need to resolve this debate to preach the letter; in either reading, Onesimus has wronged Philemon in some way, has been converted, and is being sent back under Paul's advocacy. The traditional runaway reading is the most natural fit for the text's language and tone, but the amicus domini proposal helpfully illuminates the social-legal world in which Paul's letter would have operated — the letter itself was a recognized form of intercession.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–25 — Receive Him as You Would Receive Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final movement of the appeal is the most direct. Paul names the relational logic explicitly (v. 17), writes a formal financial guarantee for any debt (vv. 18–19), expresses confidence that Philemon will do 'even more than I say' (v. 21) — which almost certainly means manumission — and then applies the final social pressure: I am coming to stay (v. 22). The letter ends with greetings from Paul's companions, whose names overlap almost exactly with those in Colossians 4:10–14, confirming that both letters were written from the same imprisonment.
verseByVerse.theology: Paul's promissory note in vv. 18–19 is a piece of substitutionary theology embedded in commercial language: 'If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it.' The theological parallel to Christ's imputation is not accidental. The preacher who has preached justification — the crediting of Christ's righteousness to the believer's account, the charging of the believer's debt to Christ's account — has the categories to understand exactly what Paul is doing here. The gospel creates communities of people who stand between each other and the consequences of each other's wrongs. Paul stands between Onesimus and Philemon's just grievance.
verseByVerse.examples: 'I am confident... that you will do even more than I say' (v. 21) — the most important unspoken word in the letter. Paul never says 'free him.' He says something better: I trust you to do more than I've asked. This is the gospel's method: not external compulsion but internalized transformation that produces responses beyond what rules require. The Christian who has genuinely understood grace does not ask 'what is the minimum required?' but 'what does love require?' Philemon has been shown what love requires; Paul trusts him to get there on his own. Then: Philemon holding this letter in his hand, knowing the whole congregation is watching. Now: any believer who has been wronged, facing the question of what the gospel requires of them toward the person who wronged them.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me. If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it — to say nothing of your owing me even your own self. Yes, brother, I want some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. At the same time, prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping that through your prayers I will be graciously given to you.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'If you consider me your partner' (koinōnon) — the noun from koinōnia (vv. 6, 17); the relational logic is explicit: if we share the gospel, we share its obligations. Receive Onesimus as you would receive me — the substitution is complete. Whatever Philemon owes Paul (affection, respect, obedience), he now owes Onesimus. 'Charge that to my account' (touto emoi elloga) — the verb ellogaō is a commercial accounting term: to charge, to credit to an account, to enter in a ledger. Paul is writing a formal promissory note within the letter itself. 'I, Paul, write this with my own hand' — in the ancient world, contracts required an autograph signature to be legally binding; Paul is writing his own financial guarantee in the letter, guaranteeing repayment of Onesimus's debt. The theological parallel is profound: this is exactly the structure of Christ's substitutionary atonement — the debt charged to one, guaranteed by another who has the resources to pay. 'To say nothing of your owing me even your own self' — the sting: Philemon presumably owes Paul his conversion; the larger debt swallows the smaller. 'Refresh my heart in Christ' (anapauson mou ta splanchna) — the third splanchna: the emotional chain is completed. Philemon refreshed the saints' hearts (v. 7); Paul's heart is Onesimus (v. 12); refreshing Paul's heart means receiving Onesimus. 'Knowing that you will do even more than I say' (hyper ha legō) — Paul never says 'free him.' He says he expects Philemon to do more than asked. The 'more' is almost universally understood by commentators as manumission (formal legal freeing). Paul secures the action through confidence rather than command, ensuring it will be Philemon's free gospel response rather than grudging compliance. 'Prepare a guest room' (xenian de moi hetoimaze) — the social pressure clincher: I am coming. Philemon will have to account for his decision face to face with Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends greetings to you, and so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary: The five names here — Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke — correspond almost exactly to those in Colossians 4:10–14, confirming that Philemon and Colossians were written from the same imprisonment and carried by the same messengers. Onesimus is himself named as a co-carrier in Colossians 4:9 ('Onesimus, our faithful and dear brother, who is one of you'). The overlap of the two letters' personnel is strong evidence for the Colossian connection. 'Epaphras, my fellow prisoner' (synaichmalōtos — literally co-war-prisoner, one captured in battle alongside another) — Epaphras is the founder of the Colossian church (Col 1:7; 4:12); he is in chains with Paul, perhaps having come to Rome specifically to support him. Demas appears here as a faithful co-worker; by 2 Timothy 4:10 he has 'loved this present world' and abandoned Paul. The final benediction — 'the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit' — uses the second person plural (humōn): your [plural] spirit. The letter addressed to Philemon individually ends with a blessing on the whole community. What Philemon decides in this matter belongs to the whole church. A postscript on the letter's later history: Ignatius of Antioch (c. 107 AD), writing to the church at Ephesus, warmly commends their bishop — named Onesimus. Whether this is the same Onesimus cannot be confirmed, but the possibility has fascinated scholars from John Knox onward: the runaway slave, freed and restored, eventually rising to oversee a major church. If so, the letter's preservation in the canon may be partly due to Onesimus himself, who would have been in a position to include it.
